chunks.goal: What do I do when a recent feature engineering or hyperparameter change caused a score regression?
chunks.overview: All items address situations where a recent change to features or hyperparameters caused a score regression, and the common strategy is to identify the offending change and revert to the last known-good configuration.

lever_contexts.lever_context: A specific recent change to the feature pipeline or input data can be isolated as the sole cause of the score drop because all other pipeline components remained the same or because compensatory tuning failed to recover performance.

levers.selected_when: The evidence points to what data or how data is encoded as the cause — either a new feature representation replaced a proven one, or a new input field was added and all subsequent tuning could not recover the lost performance.

actions.action_context: A previously working feature representation exists in the code (e.g., commented out) with known good scores, while the experimental replacement has completely failed on its first attempt.
actions.action: Revert to the last known-good feature representation by restoring the exact code that produced competitive scores. Remove all code for the failed approach rather than trying to debug it when the working alternative is readily available.
actions.nuance: The failed change is to how features are encoded (e.g., dense vs. sparse representation), and the revert restores the encoding method.

actions.action_context: A specific input field was added in a recent version, and all versions since have scored far below the pre-addition best despite multiple compensatory tuning attempts.
actions.action: Remove the recently added input field to revert to the input composition that produced the best score, rather than continuing to tune other parameters to compensate for noisy input.
actions.nuance: The failed change is to which input fields are included, and the revert removes the offending field rather than changing the encoding.

lever_contexts.lever_context: A systematic sweep or historical comparison of a single hyperparameter shows a clear best value, and the most recent setting deviates from that optimum, directly explaining the score regression.

levers.selected_when: Multiple values of one hyperparameter have been tried with leaderboard feedback, revealing a clear peak, and the current value is past that peak.

actions.action_context: One value achieved the best score and values on both sides scored worse, bracketing the optimum.
actions.action: Revert to the value that achieved the best empirical score rather than trying untested intermediate values; use this restored setting as the baseline for tuning other hyperparameters.

levers.selected_when: The regression coincides with a reduction in CV folds, and the best historical score used more folds, which also affects ensemble diversity through rank-based blending.

actions.action_context: Fewer folds were tried and did not help; the best score used more folds, which also provides more models for the ensemble blend.
actions.action: Revert to the fold count that produced the best historical score, as more folds provide both better validation estimates and more diverse models for blending.

chunks.goal: What do I do when tuning a single hyperparameter (e.g., vocabulary size) shows diminishing returns or a clear optimum and I need to decide the best setting?
chunks.overview: These items address the situation where tuning a single hyperparameter (such as vocabulary size or feature dimensionality) has reached diminishing returns or a clear peak, and the practitioner must decide whether to refine that parameter further or shift effort elsewhere.

lever_contexts.lever_context: Increasing the hyperparameter has stopped improving results across multiple attempts, suggesting the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., in data quality or noise) rather than in the parameter's capacity.

actions.action_context: A comprehensive text cleaning pipeline (lowercasing, contraction expansion, markup/URL removal, number stripping, punctuation removal) exists but was previously disabled, and the vectorizer is being fed raw text.
actions.action: Re-enable aggressive text normalization (expand contractions, remove non-alphabetic tokens, strip markup) before vectorization to reduce noise tokens and improve the signal-to-noise ratio in the feature matrix, complementing the already-explored vocabulary size tuning.

lever_contexts.lever_context: Historical submissions reveal a clear peak score at a specific parameter value, with scores declining on both sides (slightly worse below, dramatically worse further above), and a narrow unexplored region just above the best known value.

actions.action_context: The best known value is at a specific point, values slightly below scored a bit worse, values well above scored significantly worse, and one increment above the best has not been tried.
actions.action: Probe one increment above the known best value to determine whether the optimum is exactly at that point or slightly above, staying well below the value that caused a large score drop. If this also degrades, accept the current best as the optimum.

chunks.goal: What do I do when newly added features may not carry the intended information or duplicate existing features?
chunks.overview: All items address situations where newly added features may not carry the intended information or may duplicate existing features due to implementation errors.

lever_contexts.lever_context: After adding new features, the expected validation improvement is smaller than anticipated, and inspecting the feature-engineering code reveals that a feature is computed incorrectly or duplicates another feature due to a coding mistake.

actions.action_context: A feature column is assigned using the wrong helper function (e.g., due to a copy-paste error), making it a duplicate of another feature, and the correct helper function has never been exercised.
actions.action: After adding new feature-engineering functions, verify that each feature column in the preparation pipeline calls the intended function by testing each helper function independently on sample input and checking that feature values are distinct from existing features before retraining.

chunks.goal: What do I do when text tokenization or preprocessing helper functions need validation before downstream use?
chunks.overview: Items address validating text tokenization and preprocessing helper functions to catch bugs before they affect downstream processing.

lever_contexts.lever_context: A helper function intended to tokenize text contains an invalid argument or incorrect call that would raise an error at runtime, but the bug may be masked because the function is not yet exercised in the pipeline.

actions.action_context: The function uses str.split('') (empty string argument) instead of str.split() for whitespace tokenization, while other tokenization functions in the codebase already use str.split() successfully.
actions.action: Use str.split() with no arguments for whitespace tokenization, which handles arbitrary whitespace and is consistent with the rest of the codebase; avoid passing an empty string which raises a ValueError in Python.

chunks.goal: What do I do when my text scoring model uses only shallow features and achieves poor predictive performance?
chunks.overview: All items address the situation where a text scoring model relies on shallow features and performs poorly, and the solution involves enriching the feature set with text-derived information.

lever_contexts.lever_context: The model has very limited feature representation despite the input data containing rich text. The core bottleneck is feature poverty—no amount of tuning or model changes can extract signal that simply isn't captured in the features.

actions.action_context: The model is a tree-based regressor capable of handling high-dimensional sparse input, no text content features exist yet, and a full transformer pipeline is too complex for a quick improvement.
actions.action: Add TF-IDF vectorization of the raw text and combine it with existing numeric features via sparse matrix concatenation, providing the model with vocabulary-level signal without changing the overall pipeline architecture.

chunks.goal: What do I do when my model implementation cannot efficiently handle a newly added high-dimensional sparse feature matrix?
chunks.overview: These items address the situation where a newly added high-dimensional sparse feature matrix (e.g., from bag-of-words or TF-IDF) cannot be efficiently handled by the current model implementation.

lever_contexts.lever_context: A large sparse matrix (e.g., from text vectorization like TF-IDF or bag-of-words) has been added as features, and the current model implementation does not natively support sparse inputs, making training very slow or impractical on high-dimensional data.

actions.action_context: Multiple gradient boosting frameworks (e.g., LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost) support sparse inputs, and LightGBM is known to be the fastest on high-dimensional sparse data due to histogram-based splitting and leaf-wise growth.
actions.action: Switch to LightGBM, which natively handles sparse matrices and scales well to high-dimensional TF-IDF feature spaces. Keep similar hyperparameters to the previous model as a conservative starting point.

chunks.goal: What do I do when my cross-validation model selection wastes training data for the final submission?
chunks.overview: All items address the problem of wasting training data when the final submission model comes from a single cross-validation fold instead of using all available data.

lever_contexts.lever_context: The current workflow selects one fold's model from cross-validation as the final submission, so the model is trained on only a fraction of the data. An external validation signal (e.g., a public leaderboard) is available, reducing reliance on local holdout evaluation.

actions.action_context: The model is simple enough that overfitting risk is moderate, and the leaderboard provides feedback on each submission.
actions.action: Train the final model on the entire training set rather than selecting from cross-validation folds, using the public leaderboard as the validation signal for iterative improvement.

chunks.goal: What do I do when the feature space changes and the hyperparameter search range (e.g., regularization, vocabulary size) may no longer cover the optimal value?
chunks.overview: These items address how to re-tune hyperparameter search ranges (regularization strength, vocabulary size) when the feature space changes due to adding text fields or increasing dimensionality.

lever_contexts.lever_context: The feature dimensionality is changing (e.g., adding text fields or increasing vocabulary), which shifts the optimal regularization strength; the current search grid may no longer cover the new optimum.

levers.selected_when: The concern is that the regularization grid's upper bound is too low for the new, larger feature space, and the search method (e.g., RidgeCV) makes expanding the range computationally cheap.

actions.action_context: The feature dimensionality increase is moderate, the search uses an efficient built-in cross-validation method, and the number of grid points is kept constant.
actions.action: Widen the upper bound of the regularization search grid moderately (e.g., 50% increase) to ensure the optimum is captured without sacrificing grid resolution.
actions.nuance: Applied when the dimensionality increase is moderate, so a modest expansion suffices.

actions.action_context: The feature dimensionality is increasing by a large factor (e.g., due to a big vocabulary expansion), and the alpha grid's upper bound was set for a much smaller feature space.
actions.action: Expand the upper bound of the Ridge alpha search range proportionally to the dimensionality increase to ensure the optimal regularization strength is within the search space. Consider whether the expansion is sufficient relative to the dimensionality increase.
actions.nuance: Applied when the dimensionality increase is large, requiring a proportionally larger expansion of the search range.

lever_contexts.lever_context: The input text fields are being changed (added or recombined), which alters the token distribution and the amount of textual signal available; the current vocabulary size setting may no longer be optimal.

levers.selected_when: The concern is that the vocabulary size needs adjustment because the text content feeding the vectorizer has changed, affecting how much signal the model can extract.

actions.action_context: A previous vocabulary increase after adding a text field showed a large gain, indicating the model was information-starved. Another text field is being added, and the model uses L2-regularized regression.
actions.action: Increase the vocabulary size to capture more signal from the richer text, and simultaneously expand the regularization search range. Be cautious about very aggressive increases (e.g., 80x) as the regularization may not fully compensate for the dimensionality explosion.
actions.nuance: Applied when adding new text fields and evidence suggests the model needs more vocabulary to exploit the additional signal.

actions.action_context: The best historical score used a specific vocabulary size under a different text composition, and the current vocabulary size is set higher than that historical best. The input text fields are being changed simultaneously.
actions.action: Move the vocabulary size toward but not exactly to the previously best value, allowing exploration of whether the changed input composition shifts the optimal vocabulary size. Continue incremental tuning from there.
actions.nuance: Applied when reverting toward a known-good vocabulary size after the text composition changes, rather than increasing vocabulary from a low baseline.

chunks.goal: What do I do when I want to incorporate additional structured metadata fields into a bag-of-words text pipeline?
chunks.overview: All items address how to bring additional structured metadata fields into an existing bag-of-words text pipeline.

lever_contexts.lever_context: A previous experiment showed that concatenating an extra text field into the input corpus improved the score, and the pipeline already processes all text through a single vectorizer, so adding more fields requires no structural changes.

levers.lever: Input text fields included in preprocessing

actions.action_context: The dataset contains categorical or metadata columns that have not yet been used, and the existing pipeline already concatenates multiple text fields into a single string before vectorization.
actions.action: Concatenate the available categorical/metadata columns into the text corpus alongside the primary text fields, applying the same cleaning steps, so that the vectorizer automatically creates features from the metadata tokens.
